newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan sides with U.S. on emissions trading issue.
newsitem.headline: Japan sides with U.S. on emissions trading issue.

text.p: Japan conditionally supports a U.S. stance that countries be allowed to "swap" emissions rights in order to meet global reduction targets, Japan's Environment Agency said on Monday.

A delegation from Japan is in Bonn this week to help iron out specific emissions-cutting methods and targets ahead of the Third Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, to be held in the western Japan city of Kyoto in December.

Emissions trading would allow nations unable to meet internationally specified targets for cuts to buy the rights to raise their emissions from countries whose emissions are below their target levels. This would ensure that the collective target for developed nations was met, even though emissions of major polluters such as the United States -- which produced nearly one-third of total carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions by industrialised nations in 1990 -- exceed their targets.

"We agree in principle to the idea of emissions trading," said an official at the agency's Global Environment Department. "But we would insist that some definite conditions be applied along those lines."
A scheme proposed by the United States would also allow countries to "bank" their pollution credits to use later, or to borrow against future emissions reductions if they paid a penalty.

The plan would also allow an industrialised country to sell technology for cleaner power plants to a developing country and get credit for pollution reductions from the plant that would have been built there otherwise. The scheme mirrors a domestic U.S. initiative endorsed by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to cut power plant pollution by giving industries incentives to shift pollution reductions to plants that can make reductions at the lowest cost.
In the case of the United States, credits, or pollution permits, are traded freely at the Chicago board of trade.

The Japanese delegation has said in Bonn that a similar international market mechanism would need to be imposed to ensure that adequate monitoring and reporting systems made trades both transparent and quantitative.

According to a two-year study done by 37 U.S. states, curbing pollution from power plants would cost $600 to $3,500 per tonne of emissions, while cutting smog-forming emissions from cars and trucks would cost at least $15,000 per tonne.

The European Union, whose proposal would allow its own member countries to set different reduction targets on a country-by-country basis, has opposed the swapping of emissions rights by non-EU members.
But a spokesman for Japan's Foreign Ministry said on Friday that Japan hoped the EU would more closely align itself to the U.S. and Japanese view by the end of the discussions on Thursday.
"The EU still has a basic disagreement with the implementation of this plan, but we are working to forge all of the opposing views into one by Thursday," the spokesman said.
